title: Subject Honorifics: ~으시~
description: Elevate the social standing of the grammatical subject by embedding an honorific suffix module directly inside the predicate.
explanation: In Korean, honorific speech goes far beyond just shifting sentence endings (like ~요 or ~습니다). To explicitly show high respect toward the *subject* of your sentence—the person performing the action—you must embed the honorific suffix module ~으시~ directly into the predicate stem.
The choice of how to attach this honorific marker is driven entirely by the final floor of the predicate root stem:
• Open Vowel Roots: Weld ~시~ directly onto the stem (e.g., 가다 $\rightarrow$ 가시다).
• Consonant Floor Roots: Add the acoustic cushioning bridge ~으시~ (e.g., 읽다 $\rightarrow$ 읽으시다).
• The ᄅ Deletion Trap: Stems ending in a bottom ㄹ batchim drop that consonant entirely before locking on the clean ~시~ marker (e.g., 만들다 $\rightarrow$ 만드 + 시다 $\rightarrow$ 만드시다).
When bringing this honorific stem into everyday casual polite speech (~요), the combination of ~시 + 어요 smoothly contracts into ~세요 in the present tense, and ~셨어요 in the past tense.
takeaway: Remember: You never use ~으시~ to talk about yourself. It is strictly reserved for elevating others (parents, bosses, teachers, customers).
cultural_notes: Misusing this grammar in corporate settings or failing to apply it to elders is considered a major breach of social etiquette in Korea, as it implicitly demotes the status of the person you are describing.
rules: Weld 시 directly onto vowel stems, and drop any native bottom ᄅ before processing.
Deploy the 으시 safety padding whenever a predicate stem is blocked by a standard consonant.
Contract the present tense ending to 세요 and past tense to 셨어요 for conversational dialogue.

examples.translated: The teacher is reading a book right now. (읽다 takes 으시 $\rightarrow$ 읽으시다 $\rightarrow$ contracts to 읽으세요).
Mother made delicious food. (만들다 drops its ᄅ, takes 시, and inflects into the past honorific 만드셨어요).
When does the company president arrive at the office? (Formal polite question format 오시다 + ㅂ니까).
My grandfather is tall. (Can be applied to descriptive adjectives like 크다 when describing a respected subject's traits).

practice.prompt: Convert the verb '가다' into its present-tense polite conversational honorific form ('someone respected goes').
Convert the verb '받다' (to receive) into its past-tense polite conversational honorific form ('someone respected received').
Convert the ᄅ-batchim verb '살다' (to live) into its present-tense polite conversational honorific form.

title: Lexical Honorifics: Special Vocabulary
description: Replace standard everyday verbs and nouns entirely with dedicated euphemistic vocabulary when referencing respected individuals.
explanation: While applying the ~으시~ suffix works for most verbs, Korean features an elite tier of high-frequency words that **cannot** simply be modified by suffixes. For these actions and concepts, you must completely discard the everyday standard vocabulary and substitute a unique, inherently respectful word.
Study these mandatory lexical upgrades for actions performed by respected individuals:
• 있다 (to exist/stay): Upgrades entirely to 계시다 (e.g., 사장님이 방에 계세요).
You must also upgrade the nouns directly attached to or possessed by these individuals: 집 (house) $\rightarrow$ 댁, 밥 (meal) $\rightarrow$ 진지, 이름 (name) $\rightarrow$ 성함, 나이 (age) $\rightarrow$ 연세.
takeaway: Using the regular form with an honorific suffix (like 자시다 or 아프시다) is grammatically incorrect. You must use the dedicated substitute word.
cultural_notes: Asking an elder's name or age requires switching both the particles, the nouns, and the predicates simultaneously (e.g., '성함이 어떻게 되세요?' instead of '이름이 뭐야?').
rules: Swap out basic active verbs instantly for their dedicated lexical matches when an elder is the actor.
Upgrade common nouns like 집 and 나이 to 댁 and 연세 when they belong to a respected person.
Never mix and match standard low-tier nouns with high-honorific predicates within the same clause.

examples.translated: Grandmother is sleeping in the main room right now. (자다 is completely swapped for 주무시다).
Professor, have you had your meal? (Both 밥 $\rightarrow$ 진지 and 먹다 $\rightarrow$ 잡수시다 are upgraded).
My parents are staying at their hometown house. (집 transitions to 댁,와 있다 transitions to 계시다).
How old is your father this year? (Polite, natural phrasing substituting 연세 for 나이).

practice.prompt: Provide the honorific lexical verb substitute for '먹다' (to eat) in its dictionary stem form.
Provide the honorific noun substitute for '이름' (name).
Conjugate the verb '계시다' into its present-tense polite conversational form ('is staying/existing').

title: Humble Relative Verbs: 드리다, 뵙다, 여쭙다
description: Lower your own standing or status when acting directly upon a respected object, target, or recipient.
explanation: While subject honorifics upgrade the person *doing* the action, **humble verbs operate by lowering yourself relative to the recipient of your action**. By humbling your own actions, you implicitly elevate the social status of the person receiving or targeted by the verb.
You must deploy these three primary lexical humble verbs based on the specific direction of your action:
• 주다 (to give) $\rightarrow$ 드리다: Used when you are giving an object, favor, or assistance to someone higher in status (e.g., 내가 선생님께 선물을 드렸다).
• 보다 (to see/meet) $\rightarrow$ 뵙다: Used when you meet or visit a person of high standing (e.g., 내일 사장님을 뵙겠습니다).
• 묻다/말하다 (to ask/tell) $\rightarrow$ 여쭙다 (or 여쭤보다): Used when asking a question to or consulting an elder or superior.
When directing a humble action toward an honored recipient, the standard recipient particle ~에게/한테 upgrades uniformly to the honorific particle ~께.
takeaway: Subject honorifics praise the actor. Humble verbs lower the actor to honor the recipient target.
cultural_notes: When scheduling business meetings or writing formal e-mails to superiors, utilizing 뵙다 and 드리다 is foundational to projecting professional humility and polish.
rules: Deploy 드리다 whenever an item or active assistance flows upward to a person of higher status.
Swap out 보다 for 뵙다 when the person you are meeting or laying eyes upon commands social respect.
Upgrade the recipient direction marker from 에게 to 께 to match the humble verb's velocity.

examples.translated: I gave a present to my grandfather. (I lower my act of giving using 드리다 to honor grandfather).

examples.kr: 선생님, 모르는 것이 있어서 여쭤보고 싶습니다.
examples.translated: Teacher, there is something I don't know, so I would like to ask you a question. (묻다 upgrades to 여쭤보다).
I will meet the company president next week and deliver the report. (보다 transforms to the humble root 뵙다).
I made a greeting phone call to my parents. (The act of placing a call upgrades via 드리다).

practice.prompt: Provide the humble verb substitute for '주다' (to give) in its base dictionary form.
Conjugate the humble verb '뵙다' into its polite future/intentional form ('I will meet you').
Complete the phrase meaning 'Asked the teacher' using 선생님, the honorific target particle, and the humble base 여쭸다 (past tense plain).

title: Proportional Degrees: ~(으)ㄹ수록
description: Express mathematical or situational proportionality where an increase in one clause triggers a corresponding change in the next (e.g., 'the more, the better').
explanation: The advanced proportional connector ~(으)ㄹ수록 builds sentences that correspond directly to the English structure: **'The more [A] happens, the more [B] occurs.'** It tracks a step-by-step parallel relationship between two scaling situations.
Attach this connector to active verbs or descriptive adjectives by checking the root floor:
• Open Vowel Roots: Drop the ㄹ수록 marker straight into the basement floor (e.g., 가다 $\rightarrow$ 갈수록).
• Consonant Floor Roots: Append the acoustic padding safety block ~을수록 (e.g., 먹다 $\rightarrow$ 먹을수록).

To supercharge this expression and make your prose look highly sophisticated, native speakers frequently deploy an optional duplicative block: ~(으)면 ~(으)ㄹ수록. This stacks the conditional form right ahead of the proportional form to say 'If you do it, the more you do it, the more...' (e.g., 하면 할수록).
takeaway: While standard text uses simple forms like 갈수록 (as time goes on), the doubled ~(으)면 ~(으)ㄹ수록 layout delivers the strongest rhetorical clarity.
cultural_notes: This grammar is a staple in Korean proverbs, commercial slogans, and advertising (e.g., '볼수록 매력 있다' $\rightarrow$ 'The more you look at it, the more charming it becomes').
rules: Weld ㄹ수록 directly onto open vowel stems, and route consonant roots through the 을수록 padding block.
Employ the standalone term 갈수록 as an introductory adverb to mean 'as time goes on' or 'increasingly'.
Double the verb structure using the ~(으)면 blueprint ahead of the clause to mimic classical advanced prose styles.

examples.translated: The more you study Korean, the more interesting it becomes. (공부하다 takes the sliding ㄹ수록 modifier).

examples.kr: 이 책은 읽으면 읽을수록 깊은 맛이 있어요.
examples.translated: The more you read this book, the more profound it feels. (Employs the doubled 면... 을수록 maximum intensity structure).
The weather is increasingly getting colder, so be careful not to catch a cold. (갈수록 used as 'increasingly').
The better the product is, the more expensive the price gets. (Adjective 좋으면 좋을수록 contracted cleanly).

practice.prompt: Convert '많다' (to be many/abundant) into the proportional modifier form meaning 'The more there is...'.
Convert '싸다' (to be cheap) into its proportional form.
Create the complete doubled proportional block for '하다' meaning 'The more you do it' (using 면 and ㄹ수록).

title: Relative Contrasts: ~는 반면에
description: Contrast two opposing or balancing facets of a single subject within a single sentence frame (e.g., 'On one hand X, but on the other hand Y').
explanation: The advanced connector ~는 반면에 (literally: 'on the turning side of the shield') lets you weigh **two highly contrasting facts** about a situation or a subject. It balances positive attributes directly against corresponding negative costs.
Because this pattern features the noun **반면** (opposite side) hooked to a modifier, the connecting suffix must adapt based on the predicate type and timeline:
• Action Verbs (Present Tense): Universally attach ~는 반면에 to the root stem (e.g., 먹는 반면에).
• Adjectives (Descriptive Verbs): Follow the standard adjective layout: open vowels take ~ㄴ 반면에, consonant floors take ~은 반면에 (e.g., 크다 $\rightarrow$ 큰 반면에, 작다 $\rightarrow$ 작은 반면에).
• Past Tense Actions: Apply the past action modifier ~(으)ㄴ 반면에 (e.g., 가다 $\rightarrow$ 간 반면에).
takeaway: Unlike simple contrast indicators like ~지만 (but), ~는 반면에 sets up a highly formal, balanced comparison of advantages and disadvantages.
cultural_notes: This grammar is indispensable for essays, business pitches, and analytical writing where you must present a balanced, objective overview of data or trends.
rules: Weld 는 반면에 directly onto present tense action verb stems without adjusting for internal floors.
Utilize the ㄴ/은 modifier rules when linking this contrast pattern to underlying descriptive adjectives.
Deploy this pattern selectively to contrast two distinct facets of the *same* overall topic or entity.

examples.kr: 이 집은 지하철역에서 가까운 반면에 방값은 아주 비싸요.
examples.translated: While this house is close to the subway station, on the flip side, the room rent is incredibly expensive. (Adjective 가깝다 takes 운 반면에).

examples.kr: 그 사람은 일은 잘하는 반면에 성격은 좀 까다롭습니다.
examples.translated: While that person does their work well, on the other hand, their personality is a bit demanding. (Action verb 잘하다 uses 는 반면에).

examples.kr: 백화점 물건은 품질이 좋은 반면에 가격이 너무 비싸다.
examples.translated: Department store goods have excellent quality, but on the flip side, the prices are far too high.

examples.kr: 수출이 늘어난 반면에 내수 경기는 여전히 침체되어 있습니다.
examples.translated: While exports increased, on the other side, the domestic economy remains stagnant. (Past action modifier 늘어난 applied seamlessly).

practice.prompt: Convert the adjective '크다' (to be big) into the relative contrast form 'While it is big...'.
Convert the action verb '듣다' (to listen) into its present tense relative contrast form.
Convert the adjective '좁다' (to be narrow) into its relative contrast form.
